pedagogy.summary: At 7-8, mathematical argument becomes multi-step: the child constructs and follows a chain of reasoning (e.g. why columnar addition works, step by step), finds and explains errors, and — the new and demanding move — argues for why a GENERAL statement is true (e.g. 'adding two even numbers always gives an even number'). This is where the empirical proof scheme first bites: children tend to 'prove' a general claim by checking a few confirming examples, not realising that examples illustrate but do not establish a claim for all cases. Research shows this reliance on example-based justification is strong and the shift to structural/deductive argument is hard and slow. Teaching accepts examples as a starting point but explicitly models the move to a general (often visual/generic) argument, uses counterexamples to disprove, and keeps building the because-chain with connectives.
bestPractices: Model the move from examples to a general argument: 'it works for these — but how do we know it works for EVERY even number?'
Use generic/visual proofs accessible at this age (an even number as pairs with none left over; two evens make pairs with none left over, so the total is even)
Teach disproof by counter-example — one case that breaks a statement is enough to show it is false
Use worked examples with errors (e.g. wrong regrouping) and require an explanation of which step is wrong and why, grounded in place value
Build multi-step because/therefore chains and check each link follows from the last
Accept examples as illustration but name explicitly that a few examples are not a watertight proof — this is a key development, not a failing to be punished
keyRepresentations: Generic/visual proof (even number as pairs; place-value columns)
The justify → prove steps of the NRICH ladder
commonMisconceptions: Empirical proof scheme — treating a few confirming examples as proof that a general statement is always true
Convincing-not-justifying — a confident argument with missing steps, close to but not yet a complete chain
Identifying an error only as 'the answer is different' rather than naming the faulty step and why
Not realising that one counter-example is enough to disprove a general statement

learn.summary: For 7-8 year olds learning to justify mathematical reasoning: help children move from checking a few examples toward arguing why a GENERAL statement must be true for all cases (the empirical-to-structural shift). Core moves: build multi-step because/therefore chains, use generic/visual proofs (an even number as pairs with none left over), disprove a universal claim with a single counter-example, and locate and explain the faulty step in a worked example grounded in place value. Accept examples as a starting point but explicitly name that examples illustrate rather than prove — treat this as a developmental milestone, not a mistake to punish.

activities.title: Convince the friendly skeptic
feedback: When the child keeps offering examples: 'Those are all even, I agree — but could there be ANY two evens, somewhere, that don't work? How could you be sure without trying them all?'
When the child reaches for the pairs structure: affirm it — 'Now you've given a reason that covers every even number at once, not just the ones you tried.'
If the child says examples settle it: 'Examples show it works THIS time; let's find a reason it must work EVERY time.' — name that this move is a big step forward, not a failing.
For the disproof task: 'Just one case breaks it, doesn't it? One counter-example is enough to show an "always" statement is false.'
activities.rationale: The signature move at this age — sensing examples are not enough and reaching for a general reason — is well provoked by a skeptic who accepts each example yet keeps asking 'what about a pair you haven't tried?'. Dialogue is a proposed way to make the empirical-to-structural shift felt rather than merely told, consistent with 'convince yourself/friend/enemy' framing in the reasoning literature; efficacy here is not independently validated.
sourceClaims: Students strongly tend to validate conjectures with empirical, example-based reasoning (often a single example) rather than deductive argument, and the shift from empirical to structural/deductive reasoning is difficult and slow; a general counter-example gives insight into WHY a statement is false.

Specific examples are helpful for illustration but do not constitute a watertight proof; moving children beyond specific examples to a general argument (including generic and visual proofs, and disproof by counter-example) is a key development in primary reasoning.
learnerActions: State a general claim, e.g. 'adding two even numbers always gives an even number', and offer an example such as 4 + 6 = 10
Respond to a partner (an adult or a role-play) who cheerfully agrees each example is even but keeps asking: 'Can you give me another? And another?'
Face the key question: 'I believe every pair you've tried — but even numbers go on forever, so you could never check them all. How do you KNOW there isn't one pair that breaks it?'
Reach for a reason that covers all cases at once, e.g. 'every even number is made of pairs with none left over, so two of them still make complete pairs, so the total is even'
Then take a FALSE statement from the partner (e.g. 'adding two numbers always gives an even number') and topple it with a single counter-example such as 2 + 3 = 5
activities.intendedInsight: When there are endlessly many cases, as with even numbers, no pile of examples can establish a claim for every case, but a structural reason can — and a single counter-example is enough to disprove a general ('always') statement even though many examples cannot prove one.

activities.title: Build and test an argument workspace
feedback: When a case-tester stays unsatisfying no matter how many cases pass: 'That's the point — it never turns into certainty. What reason would cover every case?'
When the pairs argument is built: 'You've used how even numbers are made, not just examples — that's a general argument.'
On a sort: 'Good — to reject an "always" claim show one case that breaks it; to reject a "never" claim show one case where it does happen; for a "sometimes" statement show one case each way.'
If a chain skips a step: 'What's the missing step between here and here?'
activities.rationale: Making the empirical-to-general shift visible — cases that never suffice, a manipulable pairs structure, an always/sometimes/never sorter and a counter-example slot — operationalises disproof and generic proof. Interactive elements such as a case-tester that never turns green, a pair-grouping manipulative, and a counter-example slot are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not required tools.
sourceClaims: Specific examples are helpful for illustration but do not constitute a watertight proof; moving children beyond specific examples to a general argument (including generic and visual proofs, and disproof by counter-example) is a key development in primary reasoning.
Proficient students make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements, justify conclusions, use counter-examples, and can distinguish correct from flawed reasoning and explain the flaw.
learnerActions: Take a statement such as 'two evens → even' and run it against several cases, noticing that no number of green ticks ever proves it for all cases
Use a grouping tool (physical counters, drawn dots, or an on-screen manipulative) to split a number into pairs with none left over, then show that two such numbers still make complete pairs

Sort statements into always / sometimes / never true. To reject a claim that something is ALWAYS true, give one counter-example that breaks it; to reject a claim that something is NEVER true, give one case where it does hold; for a statement that is genuinely SOMETIMES true, show both a case where it holds and a case where it does not
Build the argument as a chain: 'every even number splits into pairs, SO two evens are pairs plus pairs, THEREFORE the total is even' — and check each link follows from the last
activities.intendedInsight: Testing cases can suggest a conjecture, but a generic argument built from how numbers are structured is what establishes it for every case. Always/sometimes/never sorting sharpens disproof: one counter-example rejects a claimed 'always', one confirming case rejects a claimed 'never', while a 'sometimes' claim needs a case each way.

activities.title: Spot and explain the faulty step
feedback: If the child says only 'the answer's wrong': 'Point to the exact step — what should have happened in the tens column?'
When the child names the regrouping step: 'Yes — that's the broken link, and here's the place-value rule it breaks.'
Keep the focus on explaining the flaw; this is not an occasion to reteach addition from scratch.
activities.rationale: Critique of worked examples with errors, anchored in place value, develops the ability to locate and justify a flaw rather than flag a discrepancy. A tap-to-reveal companion (reveal why a regrouping step is wrong, or why two evens must sum to an even) can model the target, but note its limit: revealing does not require the child to construct the explanation.
sourceClaims: Proficient students make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements, justify conclusions, use counter-examples, and can distinguish correct from flawed reasoning and explain the flaw.
learnerActions: Examine a worked columnar addition that contains a deliberate error (e.g. incorrect regrouping between the ones and tens columns)
Locate the exact step that is wrong — not just notice the final answer differs from your own
Explain WHY it is wrong in terms of place value, e.g. 'the ten that should have been carried into the tens column was dropped'
Say what should have happened in that column to make it correct
activities.intendedInsight: Finding an error means naming the specific faulty step and the place-value rule it breaks, not merely observing that the answer looks different.

constraints: Accept examples as legitimate illustration and a starting point; explicitly name that a few examples do not prove a general claim. This empirical-to-structural shift is a known developmental milestone and is hard and slow — treat it as development, not as a failing to be corrected sharply.

Distinguish 'convincing' from 'justifying': a confident multi-step argument with a missing link is close to proof. Don't dismiss it — ask 'what's the missing step between here and here?' and offer because/therefore stems to complete the chain.

Keep always/sometimes/never logic precise: a single counter-example disproves an 'always' claim and a single confirming case disproves a 'never' claim, but a genuine 'sometimes' classification requires both a case where the statement holds and a case where it fails.

Tap-to-reveal / worked-example companions model a general argument or flaw but do not require the child to construct the argument; use them to illustrate, then move to tasks where the child builds and states the reasoning.

Always/sometimes/never items, 'is this a proof or just examples?' items, and spot-the-error items probe critique and discrimination well, but a recognition-only response cannot show a child independently constructing a general argument; use these to complement, not replace, construction tasks.
When critiquing the flawed worked example, keep the focus on naming the faulty step and the place-value rule; do not reteach the addition procedure itself.
The error-spotting task assumes the child can already perform columnar addition with regrouping; if that prerequisite is shaky, address it separately rather than inside the justification task.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support general principles rather than proof that any specific activity here was tested.

The original row rated spatial/3D work 'poor' with the rationale 'arguing about number properties is not spatial.' This is a reasonable fit judgement for this topic but is not an established pedagogical law; it is reframed as 'number-property argument is not inherently spatial' context rather than a universal claim, and the 3D option was omitted as adding no distinct learning purpose here.

The even-number generic proof is sound as stated (an even number = pairs with none left over; sum of two such = pairs with none left over = even). Arithmetic in examples checked: 4 + 6 = 10 (even), 2 + 8 = 10 (even), 2 + 3 = 5 (odd, a valid counter-example to 'any two numbers sum to even'). No errors found.

The deliberate-error worked example is described generically (incorrect regrouping, a dropped carried ten); no specific flawed computation was supplied in the source, so facilitators should construct one and verify its intended error before use.

probeDeeper: 'You've checked some pairs — how do you know there isn't a pair somewhere that breaks it?' (surfaces the empirical scheme)
'Can you show why it must be even using how even numbers are built, not just examples?' (pushes toward a generic/structural argument)
'Which exact step in this worked example is wrong, and why?' (explain a flaw, not just flag it)
Counterexample: 'Someone says "adding two numbers always gives an even number." True? Can you find one case that breaks it?' (2 + 3 = 5 — one counter-example disproves)
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for a child who is not satisfied by examples alone and reaches for a general reason (e.g. every even number splits into pairs with none left over, so two evens still make complete pairs, so the total is even), and who, on the worked example, names the specific faulty step and why it breaks (place-value regrouping). Moving beyond examples to a structural argument, and explaining a flaw, are the targets.

errorPatterns.pattern: Empirical proof scheme — treats a few confirming examples as proof that a general statement holds for all cases.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Accept examples as illustration, then explicitly model the move to a general/generic argument ('how do we know for a pair we haven't tried?'); use the pairs structure of even numbers. Name that examples illustrate but do not prove — a key development, not a failing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked how they know it is always true, the child gives examples ('4+6=10, 2+8=10, see?') and, pressed for certainty about every case, offers more examples rather than a reason.

errorPatterns.pattern: Convincing-not-justifying — a confident multi-step argument with missing links, close to but not a complete chain.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not dismiss it — it is almost proof; ask 'what's the missing step between here and here?' and supply because/therefore stems to complete the chain.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child has the right idea (pairs) but skips steps, so the chain does not quite establish the claim; sure of the conclusion but the logic has gaps.

errorPatterns.pattern: Identifies an error only as 'the answer is different', not by naming the faulty step and why.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point to the step and ask 'what should have happened in the tens column?'; anchor the explanation in place value; do not reteach addition itself.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the flawed columnar example the child senses it is wrong but cannot point to the incorrect regrouping or say what place-value rule it breaks.

responseLevels.gap: Offers examples as proof and, pressed, just adds more; flags the flawed example only by its wrong answer; does not see that one counter-example disproves.
responseLevels.full: Argues from structure that the statement must hold for all cases (a complete because-chain), uses a single counter-example to disprove a false statement, names precisely why the worked example is wrong, and transfers this to a new general claim unprompted.
responseLevels.partial: Constructs a multi-step argument or a generic idea (pairs) but with gaps, or checks several examples while sensing they are not conclusive; spots the error without fully naming the faulty step (the convince/justify boundary).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask: 'Someone says, "If you add two even numbers you always get an even number." Is that true? How do you KNOW it is true for every pair of even numbers, not just the ones you tried?' Then show a columnar addition with a regrouping error and ask: 'Find the mistake and explain why it's wrong.' Discuss the reasoning as a whole; do not score a single answer.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who is beginning to prove treats examples as illustration and knows they must argue for ALL cases — and can name why the error is an error. A child on the empirical proof scheme offers a few examples as if they settle it and, pressed, just supplies more; on the error task they say 'the answer's wrong' without locating the step. Whether the child sees that examples are not enough, and can name a flaw, is the discriminator — hard to fake either way.
